newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany on course for monetary union, Waigel says.
newsitem.headline: Germany on course for monetary union, Waigel says.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Friday that Germany was on course to join the single European currency and stood by German insistence on a strict interpretation of the entry criteria.

Waigel told parliament that, despite rising unemployment, Bonn would still cut the budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, below the three percent target laid down in the Maastricht treaty.
"Latest developments give me no reason to depart from this forecast," he told a debate on European economic and monetary union (EMU) called by the opposition Green party.

Waigel described his forecast of 2.5 percent economic growth this year as realistic, saying investment and business confidence were rising, and that the European Union's council of finance ministers had backed his view.

Several leading economists and central bankers have said Germany would fail to meet the deficit goal. Waigel has already conceded Bonn will overshoot Maastricht's debt ceiling of 60 percent of GDP, due to extraordinary factors arising from the costs of German unification in 1990.
Waigel sought to dampen speculation that European leaders would go soft on the Maastricht criteria when they meet in early 1998 to decide which countries can join EMU for its 1999 launch.

"The government will observe a 'strict and narrow' interpretation of the convergence criteria at this examination of convergence," Waigel said, adding that Maastricht said that convergence must be lasting.

"We are sticking to the rules set by the treaty, from which comes my repeated assertion: convergence determines the timetable," he said. He dismissed comments on a possible delay to the start of EMU as "pure speculation" as long as final economic data for this year were not available.
Opposition leaders attacked Waigel, saying he risked becoming a hostage to his insistence on full convergence if, as they believe, Germany fails to meet the fiscal targets.
"How will he get down from the tree...that he has climbed up?" Greens leader Joschka Fischer asked, adding that Waigel would be forced to "flee into creative accounting" to meet the deficit ceiling.
The real motive behind Waigel's position was, Fischer said, to exclude Italy and other southern European states from the starting lineup of EMU.

"The efforts Italy has made to achieve the criteria are considerable and do not deserve derision but full recognition, and, above all the chance that it and the other so-called Club Med countries can take part," Fischer said.
"Your statement that the criteria come before the timetable is completely wrong. We must stick to the timetable -- nothing will get better if we move towards a delay," he told Waigel.
Bonn is believed to be keen on keeping the southern nations out of EMU at the launch because it thinks their presence could undermine the new currency's credibility.
Ingrid Matthaeus-Maier, finance spokeswoman of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), also said leaving open the possibility of delay was potentially damaging.
"The latest debate on a delay forced up the mark by two pfennigs (against the dollar) in one day. Imagine what huge problems the German economy would face if there was a delay," she said.

But Helmut Haussmann, of junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), said the SPD was part of the problem because it was holding up billions of marks in savings measures in parliament and blocking tax reforms.
"We don't want to soften the criteria or the timetable," he said. He added it was too soon to bury plans to start EMU in 1999.
